archetype.name: Pocket Passer (accuracy-first, vertical lean)
archetype.definition: A 36-year-old rhythm thrower with no rushing value who wins by putting intermediate and deep balls on the spot, and pays for holding the ball with sacks.

report.headline: Geno's deep accuracy is carrying a losing team; sacks and turnovers limit it.
report.take:
Geno Smith has been one of the league's better pure passers for half a season, and his team's record hides it. He is at 8.0 yards per attempt (10th of 47), a 4.81 CPOE (11th) and 0.147 EPA per dropback (16th). That is a sharp rebound from a 2025 Raiders season in which he was 49th of 63 in EPA per play and threw a league-worst 17 interceptions. The accuracy is not new. His CPOE ranked 3rd in 2022 and 6th in 2024, so the 2025 dip looks more like the outlier than this year's level. What has changed is where the value comes from.

Most of his value comes from throwing downfield. On 70 attempts of 10+ air yards he has added 65.4 EPA at 0.934 a throw, with a 15.6 CPOE. On the 168 throws under 10 yards he has added 12.5. The 28 deep attempts alone (1.417 EPA each, 22.7 CPOE, 4 TDs) are worth more than his entire dropback total, which is 36.7. Garrett Wilson (0.386 per target on 64 targets) and Adonai Mitchell (0.715 on 27) are the receivers who turn those throws into points. The screens and checkdowns go nowhere: throws behind the line sit at -0.233, and the tight end Kenyon Sadiq and back Braelon Allen are both negative per target.

The other side of the ledger is sacks and situational football. His 8.8% sack rate ranks 37th, and he converts 36.2% of pressures into sacks. He has always held the ball (2.96 seconds this year, and a 46.2% pressure-to-sack rate last year), so this is who he is rather than a new flaw. It still costs him in the worst spots: 11 of the 23 sacks came on third down, where his EPA is nearly zero, and 6 came in the red zone, where he is negative despite 7 TDs. Late in close games he is at -0.185 on 48 plays. Some of the shine also comes from chasing points. Trailing by 9+ he is at 0.489 EPA, but in one-score games he is at 0.054, barely above the 0.034 league average.

The recent stretch has been his best football and his team's worst. Over weeks 6-8 he posted 0.301 EPA per dropback and a 9.01 YPA while the Jets went 0-3. A defense ranked 28th against the pass has kept turning games into shootouts, and all three of those games went over the total. The low interception rate was always the shakiest part of his line given his history, and all three of his picks came in those last three games. Expect efficient, aggressive passing volume with more turnovers than the first month showed.

strengths.title: Intermediate-to-deep accuracy
strengths.body: Throws of 10+ air yards produce nearly all of his value, with a CPOE far above expectation. He has a long record of placement accuracy, so the skill is real. A 22.7 CPOE on 28 deep balls will cool, but this should remain the engine.

strengths.title: Recent surge in efficiency
strengths.body: Weeks 6-8 were his best stretch, at 0.301 EPA per dropback and an 8.5 CPOE. The offense also pushed the ball further, peaking with a 16.2 intended air yards game against the Raiders. That fits his skill set rather than reading as a fluke.

strengths.title: Two outside receivers producing
strengths.body: Wilson and Mitchell turn his downfield throws into points at a strong rate per target. That pairing gives him two places to go vertically, which is why the deep game has scaled.

concerns.title: Sacks wreck key downs
concerns.body: He takes sacks at a bottom-tier rate because he holds the ball looking for the throw downfield. That is a lifelong trait, not a new decline. The damage clusters on third down and in the red zone, which caps scoring even when he moves the ball between the 20s.

concerns.title: Interception rate looks unsustainable
concerns.body: His 1.3% interception rate is far below his recent norm: he was last of 63 qualifiers in interceptions in 2025. His last three games already carried a 3.3% rate, and he has four turnover-worthy fumbles on top of that. Expect the turnovers to drift back up.

concerns.title: Close games, short game sputter
concerns.body: In one-score situations his efficiency is near league average, and late in close games it is negative. A good share of his numbers came while trailing big. The short passing game behind and near the line gives away value.

trend.note: He opened hot, cratered in weeks 4-5 under heavy pressure and bad-throw rates (33.3% in Chicago), then posted his three best EPA-per-dropback games in a row. Interceptions have arrived along with the efficiency.

nextGame.headline: Weak Chiefs pass rush and thin corners suit his deep game
nextGame.body:
Kansas City's defense lines up well with what Smith does best and avoids what hurts him. The Chiefs rank 31st in sack rate and 27th in hit rate, so the holding-the-ball problem that drives his sacks should matter less. They are 3rd against short passes, where his checkdowns already die, but 21st on deep throws, where he has been at his best. With the Jets 9.5-point underdogs and a Chiefs offense that passes more than expected (3rd in pass rate over expectation), a trailing script is likely. He has produced well in that script this season.

Availability tilts toward him. The Chiefs are without CB Mansoor Delane (79% of snaps) and have L'Jarius Sneed (64%) on injured reserve, which thins the coverage that has held WR1s and WR2s down on a per-play basis. On his side, Breece Hall is expected back from his quad injury. That should steady a run game that ranks 19th and keep him out of some long-yardage downs. The flip side is that Kansas City allows few fantasy points and touchdowns to quarterbacks, so the efficiency may show up more in yards than in scoring.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots versus a soft back end
keyMatchups.body: Kansas City is vulnerable deep and missing two regular corners. That is where Smith's value lives. If Wilson and Mitchell win outside, explosive plays should come.

keyMatchups.title: Light pass rush, fewer sacks
keyMatchups.body: The Chiefs rarely get home, which blunts his biggest weakness. A clean pocket gives his long time to throw room to finish plays downfield.

keyMatchups.title: Tight ends against a TE-friendly defense
keyMatchups.body: Kansas City gives up more than usual to top tight ends and sees an above-average share of targets go to them. Mason Taylor has been efficient. Kenyon Sadiq has not, which makes who gets those looks worth watching.

nextGame.watch: Whether the Jets keep pushing the ball downfield like they did against the Raiders, or retreat to the short game Kansas City smothers.

restOfSeason.body: The foundation is sustainable. The downfield accuracy matches his best Seattle seasons, he has two receivers winning outside, and a leaky Jets defense keeps forcing him to throw. Expect him to stay comfortably above the league average in YPA and EPA, at roughly 240-280 passing yards a game, especially in the shootouts this team keeps playing. Two things should regress. The extreme deep-ball CPOE will cool, and the interception rate should climb toward his career norm, a process that has already started. Sacks will stay a drag because of how he plays, and he adds nothing as a runner.

confidence.note: Eight starts with a long, consistent accuracy history, but the deep sample is small and the INT rate is fragile.
